title: Debt Collectors Calling? Your Rights and What to Say
description: Debt collectors calling? Your rights under US law, what to say on the first call, how to ask for validation, and how to settle or set up a plan.

cover.alt: A phone lying next to a notepad and pen on a wooden table

keywords: debt collectors calling rights debt validation letter what to say to debt collectors fdcpa
takeaways: You have rights: collectors cannot harass you, lie or call at unreasonable times.
Ask for the debt in writing before you agree to anything or pay.
Never give bank access on the first call. Get any plan or settlement in writing.
body:
Your phone lights up with a number you do not know. You answer, and a stranger tells you that you owe money and need to sort it out today. Your stomach drops. If that sounds familiar, take a breath. In the United States, a federal law called the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, usually shortened to FDCPA, sets firm rules for how debt collectors must treat you. Those rules give you real power.

This guide covers the whole thing in plain words: what to say on the first call, what to write down, the letter to send within 30 days, how to spot a scam caller, and one costly mistake people make with old debts. You do not have to agree to anything while you are still on the phone.

## First, slow the call down

A collector's best tool is urgency. If you feel rushed, you are more likely to hand over bank details or promise money you do not have. So slow everything down. The Federal Trade Commission suggests talking to the collector at least once, even if you do not think you owe anything. Talking once is fine. Committing to anything on that call is not.

Here is what you can say, word for word:

“Before we go further, I need some information from you. What is your full name? What company do you work for, and what is its address and phone number? Who was the original creditor, and exactly how much are you saying I owe? I am not agreeing that this debt is mine. Please send me the details in writing, and I will respond once I have checked them.”

If the caller keeps pushing, repeat one calm line:

“I understand you would like an answer today. I am not giving one until I have seen this in writing.”

Then say goodbye and hang up. You are allowed to end the call, and to tell a collector not to call you at work.

## Write everything down

Keep a simple log from the very first call. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) advises keeping every letter you receive and copies of everything you send. Add your own notes with:

- The date and time of each call or message
- The name of the person you spoke to and their company
- The amount they claim you owe and who the original creditor was
- Anything they promised, and anything that sounded like a threat

If a collector later breaks the rules, this log is your proof.

## What collectors can and cannot do

The FDCPA draws a clear line. Collectors may contact you and ask you to pay a real debt. They can report the debt to a credit reporting company and sue you in court. What they cannot do is lean on you with abuse or lies.

| Collectors can                                       | Collectors cannot                                                  |
|------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Contact you about a debt                             | Call before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m. in your time zone               |
| Report the debt to a credit reporting company        | Call again and again to annoy or harass you                        |
| File a lawsuit against you in court                  | Use swearing or threats of harm                                    |
| Ask you to pay the amount you actually owe           | Lie about how much you owe                                         |
| Message you privately on social media                | Post publicly about your debt, or pretend to be police or a lawyer |
| Keep collecting a debt you have not disputed in time | Say you will be arrested if you do not pay                         |

If a collector crosses one of these lines, it is illegal, and you can complain about it, as explained below.

## The 30-day window: make them prove it

Here is the right that matters most, and the one most people miss. When a collector first contacts you, they have to give you validation information, either on that first contact or within five days of it. The Federal Trade Commission lists what it must include: the collector's name, the creditor's name, the name and mailing address they have on file for you, the amount claimed with a breakdown of interest, fees, payments, and credits, and a statement of your rights.

Once you have that notice, your clock starts. If you write to the collector within 30 days and dispute the debt or ask for verification, they must stop collecting until they have sent you proof. A phone call is not enough. It has to be in writing.

The proof should let you check three things: the debt is yours, the amount is right, and this company has the right to collect it. Here is a made-up example. Say a notice claims $1,240, broken down as an original balance of $980, plus $175 of interest, plus $85 of fees. The maths adds up to $1,240, but that alone proves nothing. You still need to recognise the $980 and the creditor's name. (This example is an illustration with made-up figures, not a real account.)

### A validation letter you can copy

Fill in the brackets and keep a copy. If you can, send it by certified mail with return receipt requested, so you have proof of the date it arrived.

[Your full name]  
[Your address]  
[Date]

[Collector's name]  
[Collector's company]  
[Company address]

Re: Account reference [reference number from their letter]

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing about the debt you contacted me about on [date]. I dispute this debt and I am asking you to verify it under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act. Please send me the name of the original creditor, the amount you say I owe with a full breakdown, and proof that this debt is mine and that your company is authorised to collect it.

Until you send this verification, please stop all collection activity on this debt. Please contact me only in writing at the address above.

Yours faithfully,  
[Your name]

## How to spot a scam collector

Some of those calls are not from collectors at all, just criminals hoping fear does the rest. The Federal Trade Commission warns people to confirm a debt is really theirs before paying anything. Watch for these warning signs:

- They refuse to give a company name, address, or phone number
- They will not send you anything in writing
- They demand payment by gift card, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency
- They threaten to have you arrested or sent to jail
- They insist you must pay today, right now, on this call
- They ask for your bank login or your full Social Security number

A real collector may be firm, but they will put things in writing. If a caller hits two or three of the signs above, hang up. Then look the company up yourself, using a number you find on your own, not one the caller gave you. You can report a fake or abusive collector to your state attorney general and to the Federal Trade Commission.

## Old debt? Check the clock before you pay a cent

Now for the warning that official pages tend to bury. Every state sets a time limit, called a statute of limitations, on how long a collector has to sue you over a debt. The limit depends on the state and the type of debt, and it is often a few years. Once that time passes, the debt is called time-barred. You may still get calls about it, but the collector cannot win a court case over it, and federal rules bar collectors from suing or threatening to sue on a debt they know is time-barred.

Here is the trap. In many states, if you make a payment on an old debt, even a small one, or put in writing that the debt is yours, the clock can restart from zero. That hands the collector a fresh window of years in which to sue you for the full amount. The CFPB advises finding out the limit for your debt before paying or agreeing to a plan on an old debt, and considering a lawyer first. A collector pushing a tiny good faith payment on a years-old debt may know exactly what that payment does. Now you do too.

## If the debt really is yours

Sometimes the letter checks out and the debt is real. That does not mean paying whatever they ask, whenever they ask. You have options:

- Pay it in full, if you can afford to and want it closed
- Ask for a payment plan with amounts that fit your actual budget
- Offer to settle for less than the full amount, knowing the Federal Trade Commission notes that settling for less can affect your credit score

Whatever you agree, get it in writing before you pay anything: the amount, the dates, and what happens when you finish paying. Do not give a collector direct access to your bank account.

Once this debt is on a plan, keep the rest of your money on track too. A simple monthly check-in helps: [Monthly Money Review: A 20-Minute Checklist](/blog/monthly-money-review/). If this is one of several debts, compare your payoff options in [debt snowball vs avalanche](/blog/debt-snowball-vs-avalanche/) and [how to pay off credit card debt fast](/blog/pay-off-credit-card-debt-fast/). And if paying means raiding money you cannot spare, start with [how to budget on less than $1,000 a month](/blog/budget-on-less-than-1000-a-month/) and [how to build an emergency fund on a small income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/).

One more thing: do not ignore a real debt and hope. The Federal Trade Commission notes a collector can report the debt, hurting your credit, and may be able to sue you. Dealing with it on your terms beats waiting for theirs.

## How to make the calls stop, and where to complain

To end the contact, write to the collector and tell them to stop. Keep a copy, and send it in a way that gives you proof of delivery. After that, they may only contact you to confirm they will stop, or to warn you about a specific step, such as a lawsuit. Remember: a stop-contact letter does not cancel a debt you owe. The creditor can still use other legal routes, such as court.

If a collector breaks the rules in this guide, complain. You can submit a complaint to the CFPB online or by phone at (855) 411-2372, report scams and abuse to the Federal Trade Commission, and contact your state attorney general's office. Your log is exactly what these agencies will want to see.

## Outside the US? The rules are different

This guide is based on US law, and the FDCPA only covers collectors in the United States. The UK, Canada, and Australia have their own rules and free help. In the UK, collectors must follow Financial Conduct Authority rules, and free advice is available from StepChange and Citizens Advice. In Canada, rules are set province by province, so check your provincial consumer protection office. In Australia, ASIC's Moneysmart site explains your rights, and the National Debt Helpline offers free advice. The shared rule everywhere: never pay a debt you have not seen proven in writing.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can a debt collector call me at work?

They can try, but if you tell them your employer does not allow personal calls at work, they must stop calling you there. Note it in your log, and follow up in writing if the calls continue.

### Can I go to jail for not paying a debt?

No. You cannot be arrested for owing ordinary consumer debt, such as a credit card or medical bill. A collector who threatens you with arrest is breaking the law, and that threat is also a classic sign of a scam.

### What if the debt is not mine at all?

Dispute it in writing within 30 days of the first notice, using the letter above. The collector must stop collecting until they verify the debt. If it appears on your credit report and it is not yours, dispute it with the credit reporting company too.

### What happens if I miss the 30-day window?

You can still dispute the debt later, and the other rules in this guide still protect you. What changes is that the collector may keep collecting while you sort it out, instead of having to pause. That is why acting inside the first 30 days is worth it.

### Does telling a collector to stop contacting me erase the debt?

No. It stops the calls and letters, but a debt you genuinely owe still exists, and the creditor may still sue within the legal time limit. Use it for peace and thinking space, not to make a real debt disappear.

## A last word

A debt collector call feels personal, but it is a process, and processes have rules. Get the details in writing, use your 30 days, keep your log, and never let anyone rush you into a payment, especially on an old debt.

This article is general information about consumer rights in the United States, not legal or financial advice for your own situation. If you are being sued, or the amount is large, talk to a consumer law attorney or a nonprofit credit counsellor. Many offer a first conversation for free.
